Here is why, what Sourcegraph is building next for developers and coding agents, and how Cody customers can plan their transition. Today, weâre announcing that we will end of life Sourcegraph Cody on January 31, 2027. Cody has been an important part of Sourcegraphâs journey. We launched it at a time when AI coding assistants were just starting to change how developers work, and it helped bring AI-powered code understanding to developers around the world. But when we decided not to evolve Cody into a coding agent two years ago, we knew that the day would come when it no longer had a place in the market. Our mission at Sourcegraph is to bring clarity and control to the world's most complex codebases. That mission hasn't changed. If anything, I think it's become more important as AI makes it possible to create and change code faster than ever. We can have a bigger impact by focusing on what Sourcegraph does best: helping engineering teams understand complex codebases, and making developers and the coding agents they choose more effective. How we got here When we introduced Cody in early 2023, AI-assisted coding looked very different. Developers were starting to use large language models for autocompletion and basic questions, but the models knew very little about the codebases they were working in. We had spent years at Sourcegraph building the infrastructure to search and understand large codebases. Bringing that knowledge into an AI assistant was a natural next step. And it worked. title: Keeping code moving with clearer review expectations | Sourcegraph
excerpt: As agents help us produce more code, review becomes more of a bottleneck. We built a bot to reduce approval chasing and make review expectations explicit.
body_excerpt: Keeping code moving with clearer review expectations | Sourcegraph Blog Changelog $ inbox subscribe --ai Subscribe for AI news & product updates Documentation About Sourcegraph Search blog Ctrl+K Blog Keeping code moving with clearer review expectations November 10, 2026 Constantin Nicolae Keeping code moving with clearer review expectations As agents help us produce more code, review becomes more of a bottleneck. We built a bot to reduce approval chasing and make review expectations explicit. The review bottleneck As coding agents help us produce more code, the bottleneck shifts toward review. Writing a change gets faster, but understanding its effects and deciding whether it should ship still take time. At Sourcegraph, we had a stamp group for small PRs. Someone would post âCan someone stamp this?â and a teammate who was available could pick it up. It helped keep small changes moving, but every request still meant finding a person and asking them to switch context. Our GitHub setup required an approval before merging . A routine change and a change that needed a detailed discussion both had to clear that same step. We had different expectations for review, but we were fitting them into one approval requirement. We wanted to make those expectations explicit and spend less time chasing routine approvals. That became our PR routing experiment. Ship, Show, or Ask We thought AI could help us decide whether a change needed another person's attention, and when. An agent could inspect the diff and surrounding code, assess the change against our rules, and provide evidence for choosing a review path. A 2021 article on Ship/Show/Ask describes three ways to handle review. We use the same distinction: Ship: no additional review is needed under our policy. Show: someone should see the change, but their review can happen after merge. Ask: someone needs to review the change before it merges.
